notes: Off-topic for this dataset: a police/retail identity dispute with no health content. Burned-in subtitles carry the whole dialogue, so it is high_text, but no health assertion is made. Collectors filed it under 'No info', which agrees.

A genuine debunking video (@dustindeanmentalist explains that paranormal 'spirit flashlight' responses are thermal expansion of the contacts), but the debunked claim is paranormal, not health, so there is no checkable health assertion to label. Tagged 'debunking' because the stance structure is exactly what the stance step must handle. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING.

@gabbituft (coachgabby.com) listing five food additives to avoid. The densest claim video in the bundle: 17 separate health assertions, several of them genuinely unsettled, and the speaker cites study years that do not match the literature (see per-claim notes). Collectors filed it under MISINFO; the section 9 rules give NO_MISINFO here, because no individual claim is contradicted by the evidence -- the weak ones are insufficiently evidenced rather than false. A good reviewer disagreement candidate. This is the strongest OCR result in the bundle: the creator displays the PubMed or PMC page for almost every claim, and EasyOCR recovered the PMIDs and titles well enough to retrieve the exact papers cited. Four verdicts were decided or corrected by what the screen showed rather than what was said, including the cancer claim, whose own on-screen source says the human effect remains unresolved. Every claim is therefore claim_source=both, and this video is direct evidence for the modality track that OCR earns its cost on citation-heavy content.

Same creator as v02. Debunks a telekinesis claim by explaining that loosely folded tinfoil catches moving air, and offers $10,000 for a sealed-container repeat. Real debunking structure, no health claim. On-screen text is only a 'DEBUNK INCOMING' sting and the handle watermark, so low_text. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING.
A mentalism performance (@jakehofman, 'Fooling my Stanford Professor'). No health content. Collectors filed it under 'No info', which agrees.

A 5.5-minute technical explainer on neural scaling laws in machine learning (OpenAI's 2020 papers, GPT-3, petaflop days). Dense on-screen text, all of it charts and axis labels. No health content of any kind. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which reads as 'nothing false here' rather than a judgement that it belongs in a health dataset; the section 9 rules give CANNOT_RECOGNIZE because there is no checkable health claim to judge.

topic: assorted health myths (hydration, joints, first aid, hair)
notes: A myth-debunking listicle. Of the eleven myths it raises, five are health assertions and are labelled here; the rest (Einstein failing maths, Columbus, Marilyn Monroe's dress size, undercover police having to identify themselves, swallowing spiders in your sleep) are not health claims and are left out. The speaker refutes all of them. Only the knuckle-cracking myth could actually be adjudicated from retrievable evidence, which is what makes this video DEBUNKING rather than CANNOT_RECOGNIZE -- see the PR description on folklore myths and section 7. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING, which agrees.
A narrated hide-and-seek competition show ($100,000 prize, six people hiding in an abandoned courthouse). No health content. Collectors filed it under 'No info', which agrees.

A Bill Nye thermal-conductivity demonstration: ice melting faster on the surface that feels cooler. Physics, not health, so there is no checkable health assertion. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO.

A debunk of a 'giants were real' video, arguing from prehistoric oxygen levels and arthropod size. Genuine debunking structure but the subject is palaeontology, not health. Tagged 'debunking' for the stance track for the same reason as v02 and v04. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING.

reviewer_notes: B: v11 c3 SUPPORTED -> MIXED leaves no judged claim, so the label is re-derived. (model-assisted adjudication) Label NO_MISINFO -> CANNOT_RECOGNIZE.
notes: [Adjudicated 2026-11-24: Label NO_MISINFO -> CANNOT_RECOGNIZE. The text below was written for the first-pass label.] A physician replying to a commenter who attacks him for endorsing seed oils. The most genuinely unsettled video in the bundle so far, and a clean test of the MIXED verdict: the seed-oil claims are supported by the observational literature, while the aside that saturated fat is 'totally fine' sits on top of a real disagreement between the 2020 Cochrane review and a 2025 meta-analysis. Under section 9 that leaves the video NO_MISINFO, but MIXED verdicts are a section 11 review trigger, which is the intended behaviour. This collector's folder carried no label.

A fitness creator explaining how she lost 15 pounds in 20 days, selling a meal plan. Contains what is almost certainly the clearest piece of false physiology in the bundle -- that body fat leaves the body in urine -- but the one paper that addresses it directly is a BMJ feature with only a one-sentence teaser abstract and no PMC copy, so its conclusion could not be read and the verdict has to stay INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. That leaves the video CANNOT_RECOGNIZE where the collectors filed it under MISINFO, and a reviewer with journal access should expect to flip it. Written up in the PR description as a limitation of an abstract-only evidence pipeline, not as a labelling preference.

A personal weight-loss account (100 pounds in nine months, no gym). Mostly motivational and anecdotal; the three checkable assertions are all either too vague to test or untested in the literature, so the video comes out CANNOT_RECOGNIZE against the collectors' MISINFO. Same pattern as v12: folk physiology that a human annotator reads as obviously wrong but a retrieval-grounded rubric cannot call false.
A student arguing with a lecturer about an un-curved exam averaging 47%. No health content. Collectors filed it under 'No info', which agrees.
A mirror/line-of-sight trick, filmed as banter. No health content, and the speech is fragmentary. Collectors filed it under 'No info', which agrees.
A natural-history explainer about the oldest animal ever found (the quahog clam 'Ming'). Biology, not health. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO.

A short scaremongering clip driving traffic to a bio link: the FDA has approved 863 chemicals, Texas has supposedly demanded 'unfit for human consumption' warning labels, and the foods on display contain 'hundreds of dangerous chemicals'. Two judgement calls here. First, the two specific assertions are regulatory rather than health claims, so under the README's definition they are not rows in claims.csv -- but they are where the misinformation actually lives, and neither PubMed nor WHO/CDC can settle a claim about Texas state law. Second, what is left is a health assertion too vague to test. The result is CANNOT_RECOGNIZE against the collectors' MISINFO. The PR description raises both gaps: the rubric has no home for false regulatory claims, and vague chemical scaremongering is unfalsifiable by construction.

THE SCREEN-ONLY CASE. Fifty-six seconds with no speech at all -- whisper returned zero segments -- and the entire content is on-screen text: 'How to know if you have ADHD:' followed by six everyday experiences. Without OCR this video is unlabellable and would come out CANNOT_RECOGNIZE with the reason 'no readable content'; with OCR it is a well-evidenced MISINFO. It is the single strongest argument in the bundle for OCR being on by default rather than triggered by low transcript confidence, since there is no transcript confidence to trigger on. Note also that whisper reported language English at probability 0.44 on a silent video, which is a useful reminder not to trust that field as a gate. In the blind subset. Collectors filed it under MISINFO, which agrees.

A careful seed-oil debunk that explicitly separates correlation from causation, cites controlled feeding trials and the Japan counter-example, and ends on obesity being multifactorial. Pairs with v11 (same topic, a doctor defending seed oils) and against the rest of the bundle's seed-oil content. Comes out DEBUNKING because the myth it refutes is contradicted by the linoleic-acid literature. Two of its claims are national-statistics assertions that PubMed cannot settle. This collector's folder carried no label.

A 27-second recipe video: onion, garlic, lemon, ginger and cinnamon boiled in two litres of water, claimed to relieve five separate respiratory conditions. One sentence carrying five therapeutic claims, split into five rows per the section 4 rule. Nothing in the literature tests this preparation, and the closest thing to a direct test -- the Cochrane review of garlic for the common cold -- concludes there is insufficient trial evidence. So every row is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE and the video is CANNOT_RECOGNIZE, against the collectors' MISINFO. The same pattern as v12, v13 and v17: unevidenced folk remedies are not CONTRADICTED under section 7, they are unproven.

reviewer_notes: A1: v21 c2 split; HDL row CONTRADICTED; label re-derived. (model-assisted adjudication) Label NO_MISINFO -> MISINFO/contradicted.
notes: [Adjudicated 2026-11-24: Label NO_MISINFO -> MISINFO/contradicted. The text below was written for the first-pass label.] A six-benefit listicle about eating almonds daily, ending in a 'natural medicine' subscribe prompt. A useful contrast with v20: same listicle format, but one of the six claims is backed by a 37-trial meta-analysis, so the video comes out NO_MISINFO rather than CANNOT_RECOGNIZE. The weaker half of the video leans on nutrient-to-outcome reasoning (magnesium therefore mood, tryptophan therefore sleep, vitamin E therefore less stress) that no retrieved trial tests. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which agrees.

reviewer_notes: C: v22 c1 -> SUPPORTED; label re-derived. (model-assisted adjudication) A4 (rule sweep): c2 eggs/AMD -> UNSUPPORTED. (rule sweep, lead-approved 2026-11-24) Label NO_MISINFO -> MISINFO/unproven.
notes: [Adjudicated 2026-11-24: Label NO_MISINFO -> MISINFO/unproven. The text below was written for the first-pass label.] A two-week-of-eggs listicle, delivered in clinical language. The best-evidenced of the three listicles (v20, v21, v22): the HDL claim is directly supported by a meta-analysis of randomised trials, though the same meta-analysis shows eggs raise LDL as well, which the video does not mention. That omission is the most interesting thing in the video and is recorded on the claim rather than treated as a separate claim, since the speaker never asserts anything about LDL. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which agrees.

reviewer_notes: C: v23 c1 referent [gluten], INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE; label re-derived. (model-assisted adjudication)
notes: @abbeyskitchen on the BBC World Service report into Steven Bartlett's Diary of a CEO podcast. Structurally unusual and useful for the stance step: the video opens cold on a clip of someone else's claims, with no framing until several seconds later, so a system reading only the first lines would see vaccine-autism and anti-COVID-vaccine assertions presented flat. The framing that makes it REFUTES arrives afterwards. All three refuted claims are contradicted by retrievable evidence, so DEBUNKING rests on solid ground. The claims about what the BBC report found are claims about a document rather than health assertions, so they are not rows. This collector's folder carried no label.

@andydoeshealthy rebutting a creator who told people to avoid Cheerios over glyphosate residues. The most instructive case in the bundle for the section 9 rules: it is unmistakably a debunking video, but it comes out NO_MISINFO rather than DEBUNKING, because the claim it refutes lands on MIXED and section 9's second rule fires only on CONTRADICTED. Glyphosate carcinogenicity is genuinely contested -- the Agricultural Health Study found no association overall, a 2019 meta-analysis found increased non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk, and IARC and the regulatory agencies reached different conclusions. The debunker is also one-sided himself: he quotes the cohort's null result accurately but omits the raised acute myeloid leukaemia risk in its highest exposure quartile. Written up in the PR description. This collector's folder carried no label.

@andydoeshealthy plays a news clip of someone claiming the body cannot break down high fructose corn syrup, then refutes it on composition and metabolism. The cleanest debunking case in the bundle: both refuted claims are contradicted by retrievable evidence, so the section 9 rules return DEBUNKING on solid ground rather than on a single thin verdict the way v07 does. Also a good test of the section 5 distinction between QUOTES and REFUTES -- the claims are someone else's words, played as a clip, but the speaker takes a clear position against them, so the stance is REFUTES, not QUOTES. This collector's folder carried no label.

A timeline listicle (@asmrsounding) about a 20-minute fasted morning walk: effects claimed immediately, after one week and after 20 days. The specific timelines are invented -- nothing retrieved tests a 20-day immune effect -- but the two claims that map onto a real literature (blood pressure, sleep) are supported, so the video is NO_MISINFO. This collector's folder carried no label.

A ten-minute lecture recording (@botanicalburr) on what 'cancer loves and hates': sugar, acidity and the absence of oxygen, with approving mentions of intravenous vitamin C and apricot kernel seeds. The longest video in the bundle and the most potentially harmful, since it points at stopping sugar and alkalising the body as ways to conquer cancer at 'no matter what stage'. It lands on MISINFO through the acid/alkaline claims, which are specific enough to be contradicted. Worth noting how close it came to escaping: its framing claim, that cancer favours an acidic environment, is actually SUPPORTED at the level of the tumour microenvironment, and the video then slides from that real biology into a dietary conclusion that does not follow. That slide, not any single false sentence, is where the harm lives. This collector's folder carried no label.

@doctorbodyhealthtips telling diabetics to avoid four fruits, interleaved with follow prompts. The best-evidenced MISINFO case in the bundle so far, and the inverse of the pattern in v12, v13, v17 and v20: these claims are specific enough to test, and the evidence contradicts them. A meta-analysis of nineteen randomised trials recommends the opposite of the video's headline advice, and the international glycemic-index tables contradict the high-GI claims about apples and bananas. Note the watermelon claim survives as insufficient rather than contradicted, because watermelon is a genuine exception among fruits and no value for it could be read. This collector's folder carried no label.

@dr_elisa108, speaking as someone living with cancer, relays a 'miracle cure' she has just heard -- blending three or four Venus flytraps and eating them daily -- and asks whether anyone else has come across it. The reason this video is in the set is the stance, not the verdict: the delivery is wry throughout ('I'm not easily surprised', 'Kind of fun', 'Let me know if you've tried it and it works'), which reads as irony rather than either endorsement or correction. Section 5 says hard cases of sarcasm and irony go to UNCLEAR rather than a guess, and UNCLEAR is a section 11 review trigger, so that is how it is recorded. Tagged 'satire' as the nearest section 14 category for ironic delivery, though it is wryness rather than parody. A second labeller could defensibly call this QUOTES, and this is exactly the kind of row the blind subset exists to measure. This collector's folder carried no label.

@drjessicaknurick taking apart a claim that Australian prostate cancer rates in 30-to-40-year-olds rose 500% in five years because of vaccine mandates, by showing the underlying data spans 2000-2024. The second clear instance of the section 9 gap that v24 shows: a competent debunk that comes out NO_MISINFO rather than DEBUNKING, because the claim being refuted is a data-provenance error that no paper tests, so it lands on INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE rather than CONTRADICTED. The video's own supporting claims about early-onset cancer drivers, trans fat and lead are supported, which is what carries the label. This collector's folder carried no label.

@drmichaelsays, an OBGYN, stitching a supplement-claims video and rebutting four claims in turn. Notable for the stance step because the refutation is often tonal rather than propositional -- 'Really?', 'the hair transplant surgeons in Turkey are really shaking in the boots with this one' -- so a system that keys on explicit negation would read sarcasm as agreement. He also says outright that for these claims he does not need to produce studies, which is the honest position and the reason three of the four rows are INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. This collector's folder carried no label.

A stitch with two speakers who disagree: roughly the first 95 seconds is an influencer arguing against GLP-1 drugs, then @drspencer rebuts her point by point. The most important video in the set for the stance step, because stance cannot be read off the words alone -- the same video contains assertions from both sides, and which speaker is talking decides the label. One row is deliberately UNCLEAR: the weight-regain claim is the influencer's, and the doctor never contests it, so neither REFUTES nor ENDORSES fits the video as a whole. Section 5 names 'two speakers with different views' as an UNCLEAR trigger. Comes out DEBUNKING. This collector's folder carried no label.

@footdocdana explaining why morning hunger is low, in four sentences. The most straightforwardly accurate video in the bundle: every claim maps onto the circadian-appetite literature, there is no product, and the mechanism is described without overreach. Worth keeping as a NO_MISINFO anchor -- a set made only of hard cases cannot measure false positives. This collector's folder carried no label.

Sixteen seconds, one piece of advice, aimed squarely at people who have just been diagnosed with cancer: cut out processed sugar to starve the cancer. The shortest video in the bundle and among the most consequential, and it ends CANNOT_RECOGNIZE because glucose restriction as cancer therapy is still at the stage of proposed research frameworks rather than tested in patients. Section 7 says untested is insufficient, not false. This is the clearest argument in the whole set for a materiality signal separate from the verdict: advice this dangerous should reach a human reviewer whatever the evidence column says, and section 9's materiality note is the right place for it. This collector's folder carried no label.

reviewer_notes: A3/A4 (rule sweep): c2 miso/radiation -> UNSUPPORTED. (rule sweep, lead-approved 2026-11-24) Label CANNOT_RECOGNIZE -> MISINFO/unproven.
notes: [Adjudicated 2026-11-24: Label CANNOT_RECOGNIZE -> MISINFO/unproven. The text below was written for the first-pass label.] @healingartsapothecary retelling the Hiroshima miso story and concluding that you should have miso soup before an X-ray. An instructive INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE case rather than an empty one: there really is a radioprotection study, and it is in mice, so the directness test in section 7 decides the row. The speaker is also careful in one respect worth noting -- he says explicitly that it did not work as treatment after exposure -- which makes this a claim with a real qualifier that must be preserved per section 4. This collector's folder carried no label.

reviewer_notes: A2: screen-only infographic claims added (c6-c8); label re-derived. (model-assisted adjudication) A2 (rule sweep): nine more infographic claims added (c9-c17). (rule sweep, lead-approved 2026-11-24) Label CANNOT_RECOGNIZE -> MISINFO/unproven.
notes: [Adjudicated 2026-11-24: Label CANNOT_RECOGNIZE -> MISINFO/unproven. The text below was written for the first-pass label.] @healingartsapothecary on getting '102 minerals' from burdock root, Irish moss, bladderwrack and moringa, ending in 'we can buy it'. Every claim here is sweeping and unevidenced, and the video still comes out CANNOT_RECOGNIZE, which is the sharpest illustration in the set of the gap described in the PR: a claim can be plainly false and still not be CONTRADICTED, because no researcher has bothered to test it. The Linus Pauling attribution row is the starkest -- 'every sickness, every disease and every ailment' traced to mineral deficiency is contradicted by the existence of infectious and genetic disease, but no retrieved paper states that, and section 7 does not permit filling the gap from background knowledge. This collector's folder carried no label.

@healingartsapothecary claiming Ozempic contains berberine, that berberine is 'nature's metformin', and inviting people with diabetes to talk to their doctor about getting off prescription medication -- while selling barberry capsules and extract. MISINFO on a cleanly contradicted pharmacology claim, and the most dangerous advice in the bundle after v34. A good case for the set because the video mixes a flatly false premise with a partially supported claim: berberine really does lower glucose in trials, which is what makes the false premise persuasive. This collector's folder carried no label.

The second screen-only case, and the opposite of v18 in every way except modality. A 'PULSE POINTS' news card (@houseofshepherds) with no spoken content -- whisper returned a single segment containing the word 'you' -- and 697 OCR detections carrying the whole story: the FDA requiring updated myocarditis and pericarditis warnings on the Pfizer and Moderna mRNA vaccines, particularly for young males. The reporting is accurate, so this is a NO_MISINFO screen-only video, where v18 is a MISINFO one. Having both matters: it means the modality track can ask whether OCR changes the label, not just whether it finds text. Also note that whisper again reported English at probability 0.42 on a video with no speech, as it did on v18. The card's later panels mention conspiracy theories, but OCR could not recover enough of that text to label anything from it. This collector's folder carried no label.

@jacbfoods refuting five nutrition myths in 86 seconds, naming the composition fallacy explicitly. Pairs with v19 and v11 as the third seed-oil video in the set, and with v42 which argues the opposite. Comes out DEBUNKING on the seed-oil row. Note that his own position on saturated fat ('fine to eat in moderation ... probably not optimal to increase to extreme amounts') is more carefully hedged than v11's 'totally fine', and the hedging is what moves it from MIXED to a claim the evidence can live with. This collector's folder carried no label.

A 24-second sales-funnel opener (@nutritiouslyeasy): day one of a 30-day tips series, recommending electrolytes in water every morning. Short, and a good test of how the rubric handles a claim whose first half is supported and whose second half is a 'long laundry list of health benefits' with no content. This collector's folder carried no label.

A food-service handwashing instructional (@partstown, a catering-equipment supplier). Procedural rather than persuasive, and accurate. Included deliberately as a second NO_MISINFO anchor alongside v33: the set needs content a classifier should leave alone, or false-positive rate cannot be measured. Also the clearest case in the bundle of a video whose claims are instructions -- 'scrub for 20 seconds' is an imperative that carries an implicit efficacy assertion, and it is recorded as the assertion. This collector's folder carried no label.

The fourth and final seed-oil video, and the one that argues the opposite of v11, v19 and v39. MISINFO: the inflammation claim is contradicted head-on by a meta-analysis of randomised trials. Structurally interesting because the argument is built out of processing steps (hexane, heat, sodium hydroxide, bleaching) where individual factual fragments are true or near-true and the health conclusion drawn from them is not -- the same shape as v27. These four videos together are the most valuable cluster in the set: one topic, four creators, labels spanning MISINFO, DEBUNKING and NO_MISINFO, which is exactly what section 14 means by covering the hard cases on purpose.
A long-form practical demonstration of the Earth's curvature, renting a high floor to watch a boat hull reappear. Science communication, no health content. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO.

A narrated scare story: a tourist drinks Antarctic glacial water and dies three days later from ancient bacteria and parasites humans have no immunity to, ending with a prompt to search TikTok for the clip. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which the section 9 rules do not reproduce -- it comes out CANNOT_RECOGNIZE, because the death is an unverifiable anecdote and nothing retrievable tests the ancient-pathogen claim. Recorded as a collector disagreement.
A game-theory thought experiment about a million people competing to win. No health content. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO.
An economics explainer on the seven stages by which global reserve currencies collapse. No health content. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO.

reviewer_notes: C: first pass kept (out_of_scope; the lobster/telomere claim is not a health assertion). (model-assisted adjudication)
notes: A natural-history explainer on lobsters being 'biologically immortal' and why they die anyway. Biology, not human health, so no checkable health assertion. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO. Borderline: a reviewer could argue senescence claims are health-adjacent, and this is in the blind subset, so the disagreement will be measured.

A two-person conversation disputing the Great Wall of China's stated length. History, no health content. Collectors filed it under MISINFO, which is plausible for the historical claims but outside this dataset's scope; the section 9 rules give CANNOT_RECOGNIZE. Recorded as a collector disagreement.

An interview with a pharmacology and immunology PhD explaining how vaccines generate antibodies. The most valuable row in this video is the last one: asked whether a strong vaccine reaction predicts how badly you would have had COVID, the scientist says he does not know of data either way, and the interviewer praises him for it. That is a speaker explicitly declining to take a position, which is what section 5's NEUTRAL is for, sitting on top of a section 7 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE verdict -- the two abstentions agreeing. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which agrees.

A 32-second clip on smoke inhalation from tobacco, marijuana and hookah damaging the lungs. Short and accurate, with the transcript garbling 'pneumothoraces' as 'pneumothoracies' -- another transcription artefact worth keeping for the extraction track. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which agrees.

A heart surgeon on regular marijuana smoking and coronary risk, explicitly answering the 'it's natural so it must be safe' argument. He gives a quantified risk estimate, which is unusual in this bundle and makes the claim properly checkable. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which agrees.

A 64-year-old creator recommending ten minutes of light movement after dinner, with a weight-loss credential and an 'I'm not AI' disclaimer. The mechanism she describes is real and well studied, which makes this a NO_MISINFO video built on a sales-style hook. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which agrees.

A dermatologist correcting four common beliefs. Contains the set's neatest logical wrinkle: he claims there is no evidence-based daily water target, and a claim that asserts an absence of evidence cannot be SUPPORTED by retrieving nothing -- absence of evidence is the verdict INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, which is not the same as agreeing with him. That row is flagged in the PR description as a case the section 7 vocabulary does not cover. It also corroborates this annotator's own INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE verdicts on the hydration claims in v07 and v12. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which agrees.

A dermatologist-adjacent creator arguing nuts and seeds are unfairly demonised, citing a University of Michigan analysis of 5,800 foods. Comes out CANNOT_RECOGNIZE: the study he describes could not be retrieved, and his other two statements are an unquantified benefit claim and an aphorism. A useful example of a video that is probably right and still unjudgeable. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO.

A four-minute teaching video on why the immune system is a memory bank rather than a muscle, walking through the innate response and then polio as a worked example. Accurate, well-structured and unusually long for the bundle. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which agrees.

A heart surgeon asked what he avoids, answering smoking, with an explicit causal claim about lung cancer and a deliberate note that he passes no judgement on smokers. The most clearly SUPPORTED video in the whole set, and worth having for exactly that reason -- a classifier that flags this has a false-positive problem. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which agrees.

A PBS News segment with a physician on measles transmissibility and herd protection. Broadcast journalism rather than creator content, which makes it a useful out-of-distribution item: the register, pacing and the closing PressPass sponsorship read nothing like the rest of the bundle. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which agrees.

A 27-second remedy clip: a navel orange coated in cayenne and cinnamon, eaten skin and all, said to relieve constipation in about five minutes, with the science promised in a description that the video does not contain. Same shape as v20 and lands the same way. This collector's folder carried no label.

A creator arguing that muscle mass built before a cancer diagnosis is the best protection during treatment. The underlying science is real -- sarcopenia predicts chemotherapy toxicity and worse survival -- and the video pushes it one step past the evidence by calling muscle your 'best fighting chance against cancer'. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which the rules reproduce.

A creator advising people not to handle thermal-paper receipts because of BPA and BPS skin absorption. One of the most useful collector disagreements in the set: filed under MISINFO, but the claims are well supported -- thermal receipts do carry BPA and BPS and these are absorbed through skin, with a measured 25% absorbed dose for BPA over 24 hours. The video is also notably measured for this genre, saying outright that touching one occasionally 'isn't the end of the world'. Recorded as NO_MISINFO against the collectors' MISINFO and listed in the PR description.

'Stop drinking water, it is actually quite dangerous' -- three claims about tap water (prescription drugs, glyphosate, fluoride) ending in a recommendation to drink reverse osmosis or distilled water. MISINFO on the fluoride claim, and a good example of the directness test doing real work: the Chinese studies the speaker invokes are from endemic-fluorosis areas with fluoride well above community water fluoridation levels, and the meta-analyses restricted to fluoridation-relevant concentrations find no association with IQ. Generalising from one exposure range to the other is the error. The glyphosate claim is genuinely partly true, which is what makes the package persuasive. This collector's folder filed it under MISINFO, which agrees.

A six-minute piece by a scientist responding to the CDC updating its site to say vaccines may cause autism, opening with 'they're lying to us' and an explicit statement of independence. Structurally the hardest stance case in the set after v32: the opening 25 seconds are indistinguishable from anti-institutional misinformation -- distrust of the CDC, a lone-truth-teller framing, no funders -- and only at around 38 seconds does it become clear he is defending the vaccine-autism consensus against the agency. A classifier reading the first quarter of this video would label it MISINFO. DEBUNKING. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING, which agrees.

'If physical activity were a pill, it would be the most prescribed medication in medicine' -- then a long list of benefits and the 150-minute guideline. The densest accurate video in the set, and a useful stress test for claim extraction: a single breath lists eight cancer sites, and another lists five unrelated outcomes, so how a system splits compound claims changes the row count enormously. Split here by outcome domain rather than by named site, on the grounds that the speaker is making one claim about cancer incidence, not eight. Collectors filed it under NO_MISINFO, which agrees.

A paediatrician going country by country through immunisation schedules to show that an official White House / HHS graphic claiming '11 injections in European countries, 72 in the United States' is wrong, and explaining how the 72 is constructed (splitting combination shots and counting annual flu and COVID doses for eighteen years). The third competent debunk in the set to come out CANNOT_RECOGNIZE, and the most clear-cut: every claim on both sides is a count from a published national schedule, which is checkable in minutes and not checkable against PubMed or WHO/CDC pages. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING. This is the single best argument in the set for widening the evidence sources in section 6, and it is written up in the PR description.

Dr. Rubin taking apart a viral 'things they told us were unhealthy' video point by point, and explaining the technique as he goes: flash a citation too briefly to read, take a kernel of truth, shroud it in things out of context. The salt segment is the best-documented example in the bundle of citation misuse -- he names the PURE study, the journal and the year, and then explains why spot urine sodium samples cannot carry the conclusion drawn from them. That is a methodological critique, not a contradiction, so the refuted claim lands on MIXED and the video comes out CANNOT_RECOGNIZE rather than DEBUNKING. Under the revised section 9 it now goes to review as a possible debunk of an unsettled claim, which is the outcome that rule was written for. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING.

A clinician answering a 'mercury in vaccines' post by distinguishing methylmercury from ethylmercury, with the methanol-versus-ethanol analogy. DEBUNKING on solid ground. Good material for the stance step because the video opens on the opposing claim with no framing at all -- the first eight seconds are the other person's words -- exactly the trap v23 sets. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING, which agrees.

A rebuttal to a clinician claiming that race, income, insurance, sex and occupation make no difference to the care you receive. Sits at the edge of this dataset's scope: the claims are about health *care delivery* rather than about the human body, and the README's definition of a claim ('X cures Y', 'Z causes W') does not obviously cover them. They are included, because disparities in care quality are a health outcome with a large epidemiological literature and excluding them would mean a health-misinformation dataset with no room for misinformation about health systems. Flagged as a scope judgement in the PR description. DEBUNKING. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING, which agrees.

A creator showing how a chain of individually-true Google answers (tap water contains atrazine; atrazine is an endocrine disruptor; endocrine disruptors lower testosterone) builds a false conclusion, then supplying the dose: the rat studies used 50 mg/kg, which he converts to 1.2 million litres of tap water a day. The mirror image of v42 and v27 -- same 'true fragments, false conclusion' shape, but with a speaker pointing at the fallacy instead of committing it. The refuted claim has no human test and his dose arithmetic is not itself a retrievable finding, so it was CANNOT_RECOGNIZE until section 6 allowed the regulatory limit (c2) to be checked against ATSDR; c2 is now SUPPORTED and the video is NO_MISINFO. Note the rule-order effect: section 9's NO_MISINFO rule fires before the 'possible debunk of an unsettled claim' rule, so settling a true side fact removed the review flag the refuted claim would otherwise raise. In the blind subset. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING.

reviewer_notes: C: first pass kept (the 'cancer proof' title is not judged as CONTRADICTED). (model-assisted adjudication)
notes: A functional-medicine doctor giving three cancer-prevention recommendations -- cut alcohol, lose visceral fat, raise fibre and drop processed meat -- and then recommending colonoscopy, with the aside 'I'm a functional medicine doctor and I will still tell you to get one done'. Kept deliberately as a counterexample to a tempting shortcut: speaker credentials and genre are not evidence of anything. This is the best-evidenced NO_MISINFO video in the bundle, from the professional category most associated elsewhere in the set with v34, v36 and v37. In the blind subset. This collector's folder carried no label.

@abbeyskitchen (also v23) rebutting a doctor who told patients to use coconut milk because it is 'the least processed'. Names the appeal-to-nature fallacy explicitly, and points out that the recommended option is the one highest in saturated fat and calories. Not DEBUNKING: the refuted claim is a processing-is-bad value judgement rather than a falsifiable assertion, so it lands on NOT_VERIFIABLE and the debunking rule cannot fire. Was CANNOT_RECOGNIZE; now NO_MISINFO because her fortification claim (c2) is settled SUPPORTED from USDA FoodData Central under section 6. As with v68, the NO_MISINFO rule then pre-empts the 'possible debunk' review flag her refutation of c3 would raise. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING.

reviewer_notes: C: first pass kept on c1 (MIXED); c6 -> INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE; label re-derived. (model-assisted adjudication)
notes: An alternative-medicine framing of heart attacks as clotting events rather than plaque events, then a list of clot triggers and ways to raise nitric oxide. The most mixed video in the set: the framing claim overreaches, several of the risk-factor claims are solidly supported, and the '2,000%' bereavement figure turns out to match a real study almost exactly -- which is why it is worth having. Comes out NO_MISINFO because the overreaching framing lands on MIXED rather than CONTRADICTED. In the blind subset. This collector's folder carried no label.

The fifth and final seed-oil video, and the most aggressive: seed oil as the single most dangerous food for the liver, ahead of alcohol, plus a bile-salt product recommendation. MISINFO. Together with v11, v19, v39 and v42 this makes seed oils the most densely covered topic in the set -- five videos, five creators, labels spanning MISINFO, DEBUNKING and NO_MISINFO. Collectors filed it under MISINFO, which agrees.

A dietitian stitching a podcast clip claiming fruit makes Americans fat. The most useful video in the set for the project's own purposes, because it names the exact pattern this annotation pass kept running into independently: start from a true or somewhat true mechanism, omit the dose and the food matrix, then leap to a conclusion the totality of evidence contradicts. That is v27, v42 and v72 described from the outside. DEBUNKING. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING, which agrees.

A two-person conversation about an anti-cancer diet, referring to an unnamed ten-year study of 'nine tumour markers' and ending on a cleanse the speaker designed. CANNOT_RECOGNIZE: the central claim points at a specific study that could not be identified from the description, and the rest is a list of foods with no asserted outcome. This collector's folder carried no label.

A creator explaining why she switched to a beef-tallow and non-nano zinc oxide sunscreen bought on Amazon, because 'chemicals in sunscreens enter your bloodstream'. A collector disagreement worth examining: filed under MISINFO, but the absorption claim is simply true -- two JAMA randomised trials measured plasma concentrations of sunscreen actives above the FDA threshold after a single day's use. What is unsupported is the leap from absorption to harm, and that leap lands on INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE rather than CONTRADICTED. The video is also careful in a way the genre usually is not: she says she still thinks sun protection matters because of skin cancer in her family. Comes out NO_MISINFO.

A rebuttal of a 'you're being poisoned' food-dye video, turning on a point of nomenclature: Tartrazine, Sunset Yellow, Brilliant Blue and Allura Red are not secretly renamed chemicals, they are the international names for the same dyes called Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1 and Red 40 in the US. Also notes the original video proving its case with AI output. Connects back to v03, which cites real studies on the same dyes: between them the set contains a video overstating the dye evidence, a video inventing a conspiracy about dye names, and the actual literature. NO_MISINFO, not DEBUNKING: the refuted claim is about naming intent and is NOT_VERIFIABLE, so the debunking rule cannot fire, while her own claim that Allura Red is Red 40 is SUPPORTED. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING.

A men's-health creator on BPA and 'PFAs' wrecking his hormones. The interesting failure is conceptual rather than factual: he conflates PFAS with pesticide residues, so the 'forever chemicals' argument lands on the Dirty Dozen list of fruit and vegetables, and concludes that spinach, kale, strawberries and grapes are 'rotting us from the inside'. That is the claim that makes this MISINFO, contradicted by the fruit and vegetable mortality literature. Pairs instructively with v60, which makes a narrower version of the BPA claim and comes out NO_MISINFO. Collectors filed it under MISINFO, which agrees.

A podcast clip claiming Fauci's text messages prove the COVID vaccine was linked to first-trimester miscarriages, and that 81-82% of women vaccinated in the first trimester miscarried. The most clearly false quantitative claim in the whole bundle, and the most consequential given the audience it targets. The 82% figure is a known misreading of the v-safe pregnancy registry, whose actual finding is a cumulative spontaneous-abortion risk of 12.8-14.1%, inside the expected range for recognised pregnancies. MISINFO. Collectors filed it under MISINFO, which agrees.

A 35-second rebuttal of the executive order splitting MMR into separate visits, ending 'leave healthcare to the healthcare professionals'. Short, and DEBUNKING on solid evidence rather than on schedule documents, which is what separates it from v64. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING, which agrees.

The companion to v79 from the same creator, answering the 'why overload the body' argument with the antigen-exposure comparison. DEBUNKING. The antigen-count claim is the classic version of this rebuttal and could not be sourced here, which is a retrieval gap rather than a weakness in the claim. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING, which agrees.

reviewer_notes: A2 (rule sweep): three on-screen claims added (c2-c4); none is UNSUPPORTED, so the label does not change. (rule sweep, lead-approved 2026-11-24)
notes: A beginner wellness-rituals listicle for women's health, starting with the Legs Up The Wall restorative yoga pose. Benign in tone, with no product and no scare framing, and still CANNOT_RECOGNIZE: the claimed mechanisms (nervous system regulation, circulation, digestion) are the kind of diffuse wellness outcomes nothing in the literature tests. Useful as the low-harm end of the INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE range, against v34 at the high-harm end -- same verdict, very different materiality, which is the argument for section 9's materiality signal. Transcription is poor in places ('managing enemy trio systemistically'). This collector's folder carried no label.

A stitch rebutting a wellness consultant who says she would not touch creatine, citing dehydration, cortisol curves and coronary calcium. DEBUNKING, and the best-matched evidence in the set: the debunker names a meta-analysis on dehydration and thermoregulation and placebo-controlled trials on cortisol, and both exist and say what he says. Also contains the clearest example of a claim that is unfalsifiable by construction -- inventing a contraindication, as he puts it -- which lands on INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE for exactly the reason he gives: 'based on what? there is zero human evidence'. This collector's folder carried no label.

no checkable claims. An 8-second meme: one spoken line in Spanish ('¡Este para vosotros!') over a French caption that OCR reads as 'enFin Te CReeR De La vITaMIne D' (roughly 'finally making vitamin D'). Vitamin D is health-adjacent, so it is not out_of_scope, but nothing is asserted that could be checked. Low confidence because the caption is garbled and the picture, which carries the joke, is not in the transcript.

A speaker on an Indian news channel recommending dry ginger powder sniffed into each nostril morning and evening against Omicron, with a pH rationale. Every claim is untested: PubMed returns nothing on intranasal ginger and SARS-CoV-2 beyond in-silico docking and a herbal-use survey. Under section 7 that is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, not CONTRADICTED, so a plainly unfounded remedy comes out CANNOT_RECOGNIZE -- the batch-1 v12/v20 pattern. Whisper heard 'sonth' (Hindi for dry ginger) as 'soint'.

@lecoinecolo reposting a French TV interview in which a public figure explains his opposition to wind turbines (concrete, rare earths, property values, 'it kills animals'). Two health assertions: a recognised 'wind turbine syndrome' disease, and people no longer able to sleep. The literature on sleep genuinely splits by measurement -- self-reported disturbance rises with noise, objective sleep does not change -- so it is MIXED, and the 'syndrome' is untested rather than refuted. CANNOT_RECOGNIZE with review triggers.

HIV denialism in 90 seconds: AIDS was caused by poppers, HIV can be 'reversed' by rebuilding the immune system, and antiretrovirals lower immunity. The chimpanzee origin is delivered as mockery ('Oh my goodness, this had to come from a monkey in Africa that one person slept with'), so its stance is UNCLEAR: sarcasm, which section 5 sends to review rather than guessing. MISINFO on two contradicted, endorsed claims. Tagged satire for the sarcastic delivery, not because the video is satire.

A self-described neuroscientist (Robert Love) holding up bottled 'baby' water: fluoride will cross an immature blood-brain barrier, water fluoridation 'has basically been disproven', so babies should drink distilled or reverse-osmosis water. Two endorsed claims are contradicted (the immature-barrier claim and the disproven-benefit claim), so MISINFO. The core warning about fluoride in infant water is genuinely contested and is MIXED, not false.

'How to choose your baby's sex, part 2': the Shettles timing method. Intercourse near ovulation gives a boy, three days before gives a girl, because X-bearing sperm survive longer. Wilcox's prospective study of 221 women and a meta-analysis of natural family planning data both test exactly this, and both contradict it. The second found fewer, not more, boys at the most fertile time. MISINFO.

A dental clinic's account reacting to a trend of painting teeth with white nail polish to 'whiten' them: absurd, could damage teeth and health, only a dentist can whiten safely. A sensible debunk with nothing in the literature on either side -- nobody has studied nail polish on teeth -- so every claim is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE and the video is CANNOT_RECOGNIZE, sent to review as a possible debunk of an unsettled claim.
external_label: no es recomendable y, de hecho, puede ser perjudicial

notes: A short, accurate summary of a real UK Biobank study (Ma et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2021): habitual vitamin D supplement use associated with a 34% lower risk of COVID-19 infection, with the speaker's own caveat that only large prophylactic studies could show a clinical benefit. The figure matches the abstract exactly. NO_MISINFO.

'Canola oil is toxic', walked through its manufacture: toxic rapeseed, erucic acid, high-heat extraction, hexane, bleaching, trans fats. The processing facts are half-true (hexane is a neurotoxin; deodorisation forms small amounts of trans alpha-linolenic acid), but the conclusion is contradicted by a meta-analysis of 42 controlled trials in which canola oil improved lipid profiles. MISINFO. A sixth seed-oil video for the set (batch 1 had five).

'You can heal any kind of disease that you have for free' by grounding your feet, with the caption 'Inflammation is the ROOT CAUSE of every disease known to man'. The grounding literature retrieved is narrative reviews by its proponents and a rat study; nothing tests the claims in people with a control group. All INSUFFICIENT, so CANNOT_RECOGNIZE. A clear example of an untestable panacea claim that section 7 rightly refuses to call false.

Spanish TV-style segment: 'Health ministry now admits more than 35,000 vaccinated people died of COVID', then a legal complaint about informed consent and the COVID pass. The spoken claims are ministry statistics framed to imply vaccine failure; they are facts of record not reachable through the allow-list, so INSUFFICIENT. The deciding claim is ON SCREEN ONLY, a persistent banner never spoken: COVID vaccines cause immunosuppression and more doses meant more ICU admissions and deaths. Contradicted by booster effectiveness against ICU and death. MISINFO comes from OCR; v94 is the same clip without the banner and comes out CANNOT_RECOGNIZE. The pair is the cleanest OCR ablation in the set.

The same segment as v93, reposted with a different overlay (no immunosuppression banner; football and Real Madrid headlines from the source broadcast leak into OCR). Without the banner, only the ministry statistics remain, and they are INSUFFICIENT for the reasons in v93. So it comes out CANNOT_RECOGNIZE where v93 is MISINFO: the same speech, a different label, decided entirely by on-screen text.

@ladyspinedoc, a board-certified neurosurgeon, discussing the reported cluster of brain tumours among nurses on one Massachusetts maternity unit. She explains which benign tumours are most common, that ionizing radiation is the established environmental risk factor, and that a single cause is hard to find. She ends speculating that there is 'some type of commonality in an environmental exposure'. Nothing in speech or on screen mentions vaccines. Measured and accurate where checkable: NO_MISINFO.
external_label: Hospital and union dismissed claims that brain tumor diagnoses were linked to vaccines

topic: nutrition / heavy metals in canned fish
notes: A nutrition communicator giving up the oil from canned fish because 'heavy metals dissolve in fat', citing on screen an Italian food-science paper (2011) on canning and heavy-metal extraction from tuna. PubMed returns nothing on metals in the packing oil itself. Mercury in tuna is mostly methylmercury bound in muscle, and the packing medium did not change its form (7185899), but neither result tests the claim. CANNOT_RECOGNIZE.

topic: nutrition / ketogenic diet and cardiovascular risk
notes: Cardiologist Aurelio Rojas summarising the UK Biobank analysis of low-carbohydrate high-fat diets (Iatan et al., JACC Adv 2024). Higher LDL-C and apoB, over double the risk of major cardiovascular events over ~12 years, severe hypercholesterolaemia almost twice as common. Every number matches the abstract, and he closes on the Mediterranean diet, which PREDIMED supports. A clean accurate Spanish-language anchor: NO_MISINFO.

A cardiologist on Spain's new mandatory V16 roadside beacons. The magnet that holds them to the car roof can put a pacemaker or ICD into magnet mode if placed on the chest; the device is not damaged, the effect is temporary, and keeping it 20-30 cm away is enough. Device-interference studies support both the risk and the distance. He opens on an alarming line ('pueden ... anular el efecto de los marcapasos') and spends the rest of the video defusing it, so it reads as an explainer rather than a debunk: NO_MISINFO.

'If you got the COVID vaccine you need to know this': a review of 69 studies and 333 patients who developed cancer after vaccination, Italian and South Korean population studies, three mechanisms, never tested for cancer risk. The two population-study numbers are reported correctly (Pescara HR 1.23 for cancer hospitalisation; Korean 1-year HRs for thyroid, lung, prostate, gastric). But the video omits that the Pescara association reversed with a 12-month lag, came with lower all-cause mortality, and was called preliminary because of healthy-vaccinee bias. Under section 9 the two SUPPORTED study descriptions decide: NO_MISINFO, with no review trigger on the deciding claims. This is the rules' known blind spot (true numbers, misleading frame), the same pattern as batch-1 v68/v70, and the strongest case in this part for a framing check in the critic (section 8).

Five seconds with no speech: a news card reading '¿ADIÓS A LA INSULINA? Logran revertir la diabetes tipo 1 y tipo 2 mediante reprogramación celular. Científicos chinos logran que el páncreas vuelva a funcionar de forma natural.' The type 1 half refers to a real first-in-human case: one patient insulin-independent a year after chemically induced iPSC islets. The type 2 half was not retrieved. 'The pancreas works again' misdescribes a graft placed under the abdominal rectus sheath. Overstated headline, but its checkable core is supported: NO_MISINFO. Without OCR there is nothing to label at all.

@malditobulo answering the TikTok trend of soaking strawberries in salt water to make 'bugs' come out: no monster bugs, at most a fly larva, and harmless if eaten. A fact-checker's own debunk with no PubMed evidence on either side (the only retrievable literature on spotted-wing drosophila is agricultural). CANNOT_RECOGNIZE, sent to review as a possible debunk.

notes: @malditobulo on hangover myths, rapid-fire: more alcohol means a worse hangover (yes); the only prevention is not drinking; eat first and alternate with water; the beer the next day, greasy food and coffee do not help; ibuprofen if anything. The refuted remedies are untested rather than shown false, so DEBUNKING cannot fire. The dose-response claim is SUPPORTED, so NO_MISINFO fires before the possible-debunk rule -- the batch-1 v68/v70 pattern.

notes: @malditobulo (Maldita Ciencia): chocolate is not an aphrodisiac, and aphrodisiac foods are an urban legend. The chocolate claim is tested directly by a study of 163 women whose higher sexual-function scores among chocolate eaters vanished after adjusting for age, so the refuted claim is CONTRADICTED and the video is DEBUNKING. The blanket 'no food has any such property' goes further than the evidence and is INSUFFICIENT.

topic: nutrition / vitamin C in orange juice
notes: @malditobulo answering a comment: the idea that orange juice must be drunk at once or its vitamins 'escape' is a hoax; vitamin C stays intact up to 12 hours. Plausible, but PubMed returned nothing on freshly squeezed juice at home (only high-pressure-processed juice in cold storage). Every claim is INSUFFICIENT: CANNOT_RECOGNIZE, sent to review as a possible debunk.

notes: @malditobulo: corn puffs ('gusanitos') burn because they are hollow, dry, starch and fat, not because they are made of petroleum. Safe ingredients, but ultra-processed and not recommended. The refuted petroleum claim cannot be checked against the allowed sources. The ultra-processed-food claim is SUPPORTED by an umbrella review, so NO_MISINFO fires first.
external_label: "¿Están hechos de petróleo los gusanitos y otros aperitivos similares? No, pero eso no quiere decir que sean saludables."

notes: Instructions to insert a raw, unwashed, peeled garlic clove into the vagina for five nights to end odours and 'parasites', because 'garlic is a natural antibiotic'. Potentially harmful, but untested: the systematic review of complementary therapies for vaginitis finds garlic has only in-vitro potential and no in-vivo studies. INSUFFICIENT throughout, so CANNOT_RECOGNIZE. A clear case where section 7's rule leaves a harmful remedy unflagged.

An ophthalmologist warning against the laser procedure that changes eye colour by removing iris pigment. It is not endorsed by ophthalmology bodies and can cause complications that endanger vision. The approval claim is SUPPORTED. The risk claim is MIXED: a 2026 case report of sight-threatening pressure rise against a 1,176-eye series from the procedure's own developer reporting no change in vision or pressure. NO_MISINFO. The warning frames no myth to refute, so it is not a debunk.

notes: @idermatologo, Spanish. A dermatologist tagged in a clip of a barber 'removing ticks with a razor' says they are black-eyed peas and the glue is visible; captions 'EATEN BY TICKS' then '#FAKE'. One of six videos in this part answering the same viral clip, in which 'ticks' or 'bugs' are picked off skin and turn out to be glued-on beans (v108, v117, v118, v123, v128, v130, v132). The debunked claim is about what one staged video shows, which no paper or reference can test, so it is NOT_VERIFIABLE and the debunk cannot be scored as DEBUNKING under section 9. notes: @danydlg, Spanish, answering a commenter who wants to buy Ozempic without a prescription. A warning against self-medication, which is sound advice, built from eleven assertions: four true benefits (diabetes, stroke, heart attack, diabetes-related death), weight regain after stopping (true), a thyroid-tumour signal (supported by trial meta-analyses), and then three listed harms that the evidence runs against -- stroke and new type 2 diabetes, which semaglutide lowers, and seizures, where the retrieved cohorts show lower risk. The stroke row contradicts her own second sentence. So a debunk-style warning video comes out MISINFO, on the risks it lists rather than on its message. Pancreatitis, the labelled risk most people know, is the one the retrieved meta-analysis does not support either.

notes: @charlotteinga, Spanish, no speech (whisper returned one 'You' over music). @lahorademiguelangelruiz, Spanish, a clip of a naturopathic speaker arguing that legumes are unhealthy because starch and protein are an 'incompatible mixture' (food-combining theory). The core claim that legumes are not healthy is contradicted by meta-analyses of legume intake and mortality.

@farandafit, Spanish. A speaker presents the Warburg effect as universal ('99.98% of cancers') and concludes that a ketogenic diet starves cancer cells into apoptosis; the persistent caption reads 'La KETO mata de hambre al cáncer'. notes: Replying to 'Can you do a video on schizophrenia when it comes to the demons?', the speaker says people with schizophrenia are 'extremely sensitive to the spirit world' and that their perceptions are not hallucinations. As proof he cites a real study (Rodnight et al. 1976, PMID:1070024, whose abstract is on screen): DMT was found in the urine of 47% of patients diagnosed with schizophrenia. He quotes the figure correctly. The abstract on screen also says 'specifically schizophrenic symptoms did not appear to be major determinants of DMT excretion', and 5% of normal subjects excreted it, which undercuts his inference. Hence speech_screen_disagree. Denying that the experiences are hallucinations is refuting a supported claim, so the rules give MISINFO with a review flag.
